title: Curing patellar tendinitis (part. 1): Causes & symptoms
summary: First of a three-part series on how he healed his patellar tendinitis. He tells how years of street basketball gave him tendinitis and how a heavy squat after a break strained his patellar tendon, then lists the causes (knee-flexion movements, friction, frequency, diet, stress, sleep, alcohol) and the telltale symptoms. He argues rest doesn't help.

claims.claim: Patellar tendinitis can be felt in the kneecap where the tendon attaches or lower, at the top of the tibia; he has had both and thinks the kneecap type is worse.
Two years of near-daily outdoor street basketball (his country had no open gyms) gave him debilitating patellar tendinitis below his right knee that lasted about two years and stopped him running.
After a break, having squatted 315 for easy reps before, he loaded 225 (felt heavy), then 275 with a narrower stance, heard a snap on rep 1, did a second rep anyway, and strained his patellar tendon.
His strain happened because he went too heavy after a break before his muscles caught up, made far worse by pre-existing tendinitis; after a layoff you must be patient with lost strength.
His doctor's drugs and prescribed movements didn't cure his tendinitis; he healed it himself through weightlifting (disclaimer: he's not a doctor).
Squats are the main cause of knee problems for lifters, but leg extensions, leg curls, split squats and lunges can also damage the knee.

Before a tendon snaps, inflammation and tendinitis come first, often from the tendon rubbing against bone or cartilage due to an individual squat pattern; whatever the mechanics, pain when squatting means something is wrong and you should stop.
Diet and lifestyle (stress, lack of sleep, alcohol) promote inflammation and make tendon damage more likely; his injury came during a very stressful period, and the injury added more stress.
He never does lunges: even with proper form they inflame his knees. If squats hurt you, play with stance and foot position.
Even perfect squat form will wear down your tendons if frequency is too high for you to recover.
He doesn't recommend rest for patellar tendinitis: it's caused by a movement pattern you'll repeat, and resting can make it worse.
Telltale sign: it hurts on light warm-up squat sets but the pain fades once the area is pumped and warm; pain that keeps increasing as you squat suggests a tear or something else.
Tendinitis gets worse in the cold, with atmospheric pressure changes (e.g. flying), and when not warmed up: pain at night or stiffness on waking.
Going up stairs hurts more than going down; the knee is tender to press and feels warm after training; rolling the kneecap hurts with the kneecap type.
His tibia-level tendinitis disappeared when he stopped basketball, but the kneecap type flares with any knee flexion.
With kneecap tendinitis it's the moment of breaking at the knee that hurts, not the rest of the descent or ascent; it can affect deadlifts even more than squats.

A key symptom: the knee suddenly gives way when walking, a protective reflex where the body refuses to lock a weak tendon under load, then you walk normally a second later; this happened to him all the time.
He fixed his tendinitis through weightlifting, not rest or anti-inflammatory pills; the methods come in part 2.
